segments.title: Haida and the Tribal-class ships that were not preserved
segments.summary: Seeing HMCS Haida for the first time prompts a reflection on distinguished Tribal-class destroyers lost in war or sent to the breakers.
segments.body: Haida's survival feels exceptional because several other Tribals also deserved preservation. Nubian is singled out for her battle honours, Eskimo survived the loss of her bow, and Tartar is remembered as a very good, happy ship. None of those three survived the breakers' yards. Their fate sets the emotional force of seeing Haida against the much larger part of the class preserved only in records and memory.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke sees Haida, then discusses Nubian, Eskimo, Tartar, and the loss of the other ships to war or scrapping.

segments.title: Why ocean-going destroyers had to be large
segments.summary: Haida's physical scale shows why destroyers serving fast fleets across Atlantic and Pacific distances could not be truly small ships.
segments.body: Haida's size directly challenges the usual description of destroyers as a navy's little ships. From the quayside, her hull dwarfs someone just under six feet tall. Atlantic and Pacific distances required a substantial hull that could operate with fast carriers and capital ships. Her scale follows from the range and speed needed to protect those fleet units across vast oceans.

evidence.note: He contrasts the destroyer's imposing size with the little-ships label and ties that size to ocean operations with fast fleet units.

segments.title: Tribal-class forward firepower in destroyer combat
segments.summary: The Tribal class combined a threatening head-on silhouette with rapid forward gunfire intended to overwhelm enemy destroyers and engage light cruisers.
segments.body: Haida's appearance suggests how four Tribal-class destroyers and the British-built Polish destroyer ORP Piorun would have looked bearing down on Bismarck in darkness. At Narvik, Tribals could approach head-on while keeping as many forward guns on target as an opposing destroyer carried in total. Their guns fired faster as well, giving them the weight of fire to overwhelm enemy destroyers. The class was also intended to fight light cruisers, especially Italian ships, and Cape Bon is given as an example of success in that role.

evidence.note: He describes the Tribals' forward guns, rate-of-fire advantage, and intended role overwhelming destroyers and light cruisers.

segments.title: Tribal-class losses and wartime mission overload
segments.summary: Heavy Tribal-class losses are connected to a fleet-wide shortage that pushed the ships into too many demanding missions.
segments.body: Severe wartime attrition affected the 27 Tribal-class destroyers, including Royal Navy and Canadian ships. Those losses are presented as more than a verdict on the design. The ships were repeatedly committed because the fleet lacked enough destroyers and cruisers to cover every task. Their heavy employment shows how a shortage of light forces can push a capable class into missions beyond the role for which it was optimized.

evidence.note: The transcript emphasizes the class's heavy wartime losses and attributes its demanding employment to shortages of destroyers and cruisers.
